WorkedExamples.Question: On one side of a straight line lie three adjacent angles labeled a, 90°, b. Is the information enough to find a and b individually?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw an independent accurate geometry model, measure or construct required angles/sides/cross-sections, calculate and justify, and submit for teacher review.
Steps: The straight total gives a+90+b=180, hence a+b=90.

WorkedExamples.Answer: Not enough for unique a,b; only a+b=90° is known.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks two distinct geometric realizations and explanation of underdetermination.

Lessons.Title: Building Polygons (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks goal: Explore which side and angle conditions determine a polygon and whether different solutions exist. Independent lesson examples with 2017–2019 OUR/IM historical preparation source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/7/6/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 attribution; no copied illustrations or assessments).

Grade 7 source-sequence repair: In this lesson, first build hinged polygons using fixed strip lengths, measure and redraw a triangle and a quadrilateral, and compare overlapping copies. Four fixed side lengths can allow different quadrilaterals; three feasible fixed side lengths determine one triangle up to congruence. Use 4 in, 5 in, 6 in and 9 in for two different quadrilaterals and 4 in, 5 in, 8 in for a closing triangle. Treat 3 in, 4 in and 9 in as a failed physical closure. Defer the general triangle-inequality rule and compass endpoint-circle construction to the following lesson U07:L07, rather than replacing this investigation with a numerical shortcut. Student source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/7/6/index.html.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent geometric problem 1
WorkedExamples.Question: A triangle has sides 3,4,5. Is it possible?
WorkedExamples.Method: Physically join three labeled strips, check whether the endpoints close to a triangle, and compare the finished shape with a peer.
Steps: Join 3 cm and 4 cm strips at one endpoint; try to join their free endpoints using the 5 cm strip.
A non-flat triangular construction closes; draw and measure it.
With these three fixed lengths another copy may be turned or flipped, but it matches in shape and size.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use geometric invariants, substitution or physical construction evidence; teacher review for drawing quality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent geometric problem 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Could sides 2,3,6 form a triangle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Try to close three strips physically; when they cannot meet, explain the endpoint gap rather than relying only on an unintroduced general rule.
Steps: Join the 2 cm and 3 cm strips end-to-end to maximize their reach; together they span at most 5 cm.
The remaining strip is 6 cm long, so the two ends cannot meet to form a non-flat triangle.
Record the failed closure and compare this reasoning with the constructions from the first task.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use geometric invariants, substitution or physical construction evidence; teacher review for drawing quality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent geometric problem 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Two rectangles each have perimeter 20 cm; one is 4 by 6, another 3 by 7. Are they identical?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the relevant geometric relation and verify all measurements and constraints.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; equal perimeter does not force congruence.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use geometric invariants, substitution or physical construction evidence; teacher review for drawing quality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct and justify — Building Polygons (Part 1)
WorkedExamples.Question: Use sticks of lengths 4, 5, 8 cm to make a triangle and sticks 3, 4, 9 cm to try making a triangle. Explain outcomes, then draw a nonunique four-side example.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw an independent accurate geometry model, measure or construct required angles/sides/cross-sections, calculate and justify, and submit for teacher review.
Steps: Make a triangle with hinged 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm strips; measure and sketch its angles, then compare copies.
Try hinged strips of 3 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm; even when the shorter strips point in the same direction, they leave a gap.
Make two quadrilaterals with consecutive sides 9, 4, 5 and 6 inches, allowing the hinge angle to change; record different diagonal lengths such as 7 and 9 inches.
Overlay the two quadrilaterals to show they are not identical, despite the same four side lengths. Explain why any 4-5-8 triangles from fixed rigid strips overlay after rotation or reflection.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A 4-5-8 triangle exists; 3-4-9 is impossible; quadrilateral side-only data can be nonunique.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews actual hinged models, accurate side and angle measurements, overlay comparison and descriptions. Do not auto-pass an answer based on an arithmetic inequality alone.

ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks goal: Classify whether three given measurements ensure identical triangles or permit different triangles. Independent lesson examples with 2017–2019 OUR/IM historical preparation source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/7/8/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 attribution; no copied illustrations or assessments).

Source-specific side-position repair: Compare three given measurements in their actual positions, then decide whether two differently oriented drawings can be overlaid. A triangle with angles 40°, 60°, 80° and length 5 between the 40° and 60° vertices is NOT the same size as a triangle with length 5 between the 40° and 80° vertices. Measure and compare corresponding sides and explain the adjacency difference. A rotation/reflection is an identical copy, not a new triangle. This lesson develops concrete reasoning; memorizing SSS, SAS, ASA or AAA names is not a required student objective. Source student: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/7/8/index.html.

KeyConcepts.Title: Core geometric idea
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three feasible matching side lengths give an identical triangle shape, even if drawn in different orientations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check corresponding lengths and whether two triangles overlay after rigid movement, not just their page orientation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rule and representation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two sides and an angle must be matched in their corresponding positions; a non-included angle can allow different figures.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identify which measured angle lies between the given sides and compare actual neighboring parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three given angles alone do not determine scale, and two angles plus one side require that the side's position be specified.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare location of the marked side relative to the vertices with known angles before declaring identical copies.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent geometric problem 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Triangle A has sides 3,4,5 and B also 3,4,5. Are they congruent?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the relevant geometric relation and verify all measurements and constraints.
Steps: Label corresponding sides 3,4,5 on both triangles.
Rotate or flip one construction if needed; every pair of matching lengths overlays.
Conclude the two shapes are identical copies, regardless of how they face on the page.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use geometric invariants, substitution or physical construction evidence; teacher review for drawing quality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent geometric problem 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Two triangles both have angles 40°,60°,80°. Must they be congruent?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the relevant geometric relation and verify all measurements and constraints.
Steps: Confirm the two angle sets each contain 40°, 60°, and 80°.
Trace one triangle and draw a second copy twice as large while keeping the same angle measures.
They are not identical copies; angle equality alone does not fix the side lengths.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use geometric invariants, substitution or physical construction evidence; teacher review for drawing quality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent geometric problem 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Do sides 4,4,9 define a triangle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the relevant geometric relation and verify all measurements and constraints.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use geometric invariants, substitution or physical construction evidence; teacher review for drawing quality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct and justify — Triangles with 3 Common Measures
WorkedExamples.Question: Two triangles each have interior angles 50°,60°,70°, but one has a 3 cm side and another the corresponding side is 6 cm. Are they identical? What additional type of measurement fixes size?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw an independent accurate geometry model, measure or construct required angles/sides/cross-sections, calculate and justify, and submit for teacher review.
Steps: Identical corresponding angles determine similarity but not absolute scale.
A 6 cm corresponding side is twice the 3 cm side, so the triangles are not congruent.
Specifying one corresponding side alongside the matching angles fixes overall size up to congruence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct and justify — Building Prisms
WorkedExamples.Question: A right triangular prism has a 3–4–5 cm right-triangle base and prism length 8 cm. Draw a net, compute volume and exterior area, and state a possible horizontal cross-section.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw an independent accurate geometry model, measure or construct required angles/sides/cross-sections, calculate and justify, and submit for teacher review.
Steps: The two matching triangular bases each have area (3×4)/2=6 cm².
Wrap three lateral rectangles 3×8,4×8,5×8 cm around the triangle; lateral area=96 cm².
Total surface area=2×6+96=108 cm²; volume=6×8=48 cm³.
Draw both triangles and all three correctly connected rectangular panels; slice parallel to the triangular bases gives a congruent triangle.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Volume 48 cm³, surface 108 cm²; parallel cross-section a 3–4–5 triangle.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the assembled net dimensions, foldability and actual geometric cross-section.
